text:
SASRec already carries same-position information through residual connections, uses shared input/output item embeddings, and scores candidates with the final Transformer state. Its reference implementation scales input embeddings by √d and applies final LayerNorm; this does not imply that an additional raw-embedding residual has a matched norm. [SASRec implementation](https://github.com/kang205/SASRec/blob/master/model.py). The closest Transformer/pooling precedent is CORE-trm: Transformer features produce softmax weights over history, then those weights combine the original item embeddings. CORE-ave supplies a uniform, whole-session mean baseline. Both normalize the pooled representation and candidate embeddings and use temperature-scaled cosine logits; neither implements an additive SASRec-plus-recent-mean residual. [CORE implementation](https://github.com/RUCAIBox/CORE).

Related precedents establish the broader recent-interest idea. STAMP explicitly combines session-context interests with last-click interests, but is not a Transformer model. [STAMP](https://www.kdd.org/kdd2018/accepted-papers/view/stamp-short-term-attentionmemory-priority-model-for-session-based-recommend). HGN applies learned sigmoid gates at feature and interaction levels, pools recent embeddings, and adds explicit item–item scores alongside user and pooled-interest scores. Its input/output item tables are separate; its gates select information rather than control a Transformer residual coefficient. [HGN paper](https://arxiv.org/html/1906.09217).

For the proposed tied-embedding residual, a defensible experimental design is h′=h+α·Norm(mean(last-k embeddings)), with branch normalization and scalar or contextual gating evaluated separately. This is a recommendation, not a formula established by those papers. Compare unchanged SASRec, residual-only scoring, last-item k=1, several recent windows, whole-history mean, and CORE-style weighted pooling; compare fixed versus learned α and raw versus normalized branches. Report branch norms and learned gate values. CORE’s mean-versus-Transformer comparison supports testing pooling, but does not establish that a recent window beats longer-history pooling.
